young.html: Long ago in Rome, a great general named Julius Caesar became so powerful that some Romans feared he would make himself king. A group of senators, led by Cassius and Caesar's friend Brutus, plotted to stop him.

On the Ides of March, the 15th, they killed him. Brutus told the crowd he had done it to keep Rome free. Then Caesar's friend Mark Antony gave a speech so clever that the crowd turned against the plotters. A war followed, and the plotters lost.

young.text:
Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears;
I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him.
young.author: William Shakespeare
young.work: Julius Caesar, Act III, scene 2 (Mark Antony)
young.ed: First printed in the First Folio
young.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

young.html: Shakespeare found this true story in a book by the Greek writer Plutarch, who lived about 1,500 years before him.

Two speeches. After the murder, Brutus speaks plainly and asks the crowd to think. Antony speaks with feeling and shows them Caesar's cloak. Pick a simple question (should we get a dog?) and give two short speeches, one with reasons only and one with feelings. Which persuades your family more?
young.title: Try this: reason or feeling?

full.html: Shakespeare wrote Julius Caesar in 1599; a Swiss visitor, Thomas Platter, saw it acted on Bankside that September, probably at the new Globe. His source was Plutarch's Lives of Caesar, Brutus and Antony, in Thomas North's English translation (1579), on an earlier rung of this ladder. The real murder took place in 44 BC.

full.cap: The five acts. The title character dies in the middle of the play.

full.text:
Men at some time are masters of their fates:
The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars,
But in ourselves, that we are underlings.
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.ed: First printed in the First Folio
full.note: "Underlings" means people of lower rank. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: Cassius works on Brutus with arguments and with forged letters from "citizens." Brutus, a man of honor, decides alone in his orchard that Caesar must die, not for what he is but for what power might make him. Readers have argued ever since whether Brutus is a hero of liberty, a traitor to a friend, or a good man who reasons himself into a terrible act.

Brutus speaks first, in prose, and appeals to the crowd's reason and to his own honor: "Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more." Then he lets Antony speak, against Cassius's advice. Antony, in verse, praises Brutus as "an honourable man" again and again until the phrase turns bitter, shows the crowd Caesar's wounds and cloak, and reads his will. The crowd riots.

full.html: Later Shakespeare returned to Plutarch for Antony and Cleopatra (c. 1606), the love and fall of Mark Antony and the queen of Egypt, and Coriolanus (c. 1608), a proud general of early Rome who scorns the people. These plays deal with mature themes; the summaries here are enough for young readers.
Thinking Caesar is the hero because the play has his name. Brutus has far more lines, and many critics see him as the tragic hero.

deep.html: Julius Caesar shows how speech moves crowds, and how easily. Aristotle's Rhetoric, earlier on this ladder, names the tools both men use. The play stays neutral between them: Brutus is right that persuasion should be reasoned, and wrong about what moves people.

items: Can it ever be right to kill a leader to protect a republic? What does the play suggest, and what do you think?
Is Cassius right that the fault is "in ourselves" and not in fate?
Why does reason lose to feeling in the Forum? Should it?

questions: Brutus says he loved Rome more than Caesar. Can loyalty to a cause ever be more important than loyalty to a friend?
Who gave the better speech, Brutus or Antony? Which was more honest?
Cassius says "The fault ... is not in our stars, / But in ourselves." Do you agree?
Why do you think crowds can change their minds so quickly?
care: The play shows an assassination and a civil war, and several characters take their own lives after defeat. This lesson states this plainly without detail.
